text: Lesson twenty-six got you a yes. The temptation now is to go big immediately — full operating model, every role, a complete policy library, company-wide, all at once. Resist that. Start with a pilot.

Scaling governance too fast scales your mistakes right along with it — a confusing RACI, an unrealistic policy, a tool nobody adopted. A pilot finds those mistakes while the cost of being wrong is still small. And it produces a true story — a specific, measurable win — far more persuasive than any framework diagram.

Not every domain makes an equally good pilot. Three criteria, used together: high value, so a win is worth talking about. High pain, so stakeholders already feel the problem and show up engaged. And high feasibility — small enough that a small team can actually finish in a defined window.

A real pilot needs five pieces. A defined objective, in one sentence. A baseline measurement, captured before anything changes. A named owner — an actual person, not an abstract team. A fixed time window, typically sixty to ninety days. And a planned decision point at the end: scale it, adjust it, or stop it.

Four ways pilots fail even when the idea was sound: too ambitious a scope that fails the feasibility test, no executive visibility so a real win has no audience, no baseline so there's nothing to compare against, and no defined end so it just drifts.

High value, high pain, high feasibility — five pieces, a fixed window, a real decision at the end. That's a pilot built to actually prove something. Next up: how a successful pilot becomes a full roadmap.
